summary: English -ing is several different things in Italian. Stare + gerundio (sto mangiando) is only for an action in progress right now or at that moment; stare per + infinitive is about to. Where -ing names an activity, Italian uses the infinitive (mi piace leggere); where it describes a noun, a relative clause (la ragazza che parla). The bare gerund says how, why or while the subject itself acts.

subs.label: sto mangiando, stavo dormendo: action in progress
subs.focus: Stare in the presente or imperfetto + invariable gerund for an action going on at this moment or at that past moment. Typical errors: essere for stare (Sono mangiando), a compound tense of stare (Sono stato lavorando tutto il giorno; Italian says Ho lavorato tutto il giorno), and an agreeing gerund (Stanno mangiandi). The simple presente and imperfetto can also describe an action in progress (Che fai? Mangio.), so items must not mark the simple tense wrong for an ongoing action: test the form of stare, the choice stare against essere, or the gerund after a given sto / stavo, and use adesso, in questo momento, proprio ora or a quando-clause to fix the moment. Stare + gerundio also exists in other simple tenses (starà dormendo); items stay in the presente and imperfetto.

subs.label: -ando / -endo, facendo, dicendo, bevendo
subs.focus: Verbs in -are take -ando; verbs in -ere and -ire take -endo, and -ire verbs with -isc- do not keep it (finendo, capendo). A few verbs build the gerund on their longer old stem, such as fare: facendo, dire: dicendo, bere: bevendo, tradurre: traducendo. The gerund has one form for every person and gender. Typical errors: -indo or -iendo on -ire verbs (partindo, dormiendo), -ando on -ere verbs (leggiando), finiscendo, farendo / fando, direndo, berendo. Items test the form inside stare + gerundio or a bare-gerund sentence with the infinitive given.

subs.label: domani parto, lo so: where English be + -ing is not stare + gerundio
subs.focus: English uses be + -ing for future plans and for some states; Italian does not. A plan or arrangement with a future time takes the presente or the futuro (Domani parto per Roma, not Sto partendo domani). Verbs of state such as sapere, conoscere, volere, potere, dovere, essere and avere for possession are not normally put in stare + gerundio (So la risposta; Avevo una macchina rossa). English is wearing, is sitting, is standing describe a state and take a simple verb or essere + participle (Porta una giacca blu; È seduto in giardino). Typical error: translating every am / is / are / was + -ing with stare + gerundio. Items need a future time word, or a clearly stative verb, so that only the simple tense is right; do not use pensare, avere problemi, sentirsi or other verbs that do accept stare + gerundio as wrong answers.

subs.label: sto per uscire: about to
subs.focus: Stare per + infinitive says the action has not started but is about to; in the imperfetto it says was about to, often of something that then did not happen or was interrupted (Stavo per uscire quando ha telefonato Anna). Typical errors: the gerund after per (Sto per uscendo), essere for stare (Sono per uscire), and confusing the two stare constructions: Il film sta cominciando (it is starting now) against Il film sta per cominciare (it has not started yet). Items must give a cue such as tra un minuto, non ancora, sbrigati for about to, or già, adesso for in progress.

subs.label: nuotare fa bene, mi piace leggere, senza parlare: -ing as an activity
subs.focus: When English -ing names an activity (as subject, as object of a verb, or after a preposition), Italian uses the infinitive, never the gerund: Fumare fa male; Mi piace cucinare; Ho smesso di fumare; È uscito senza salutare. Typical error: the gerund in all three places (Fumando fa male; Mi piace cucinando; Ho smesso di fumando; senza salutando). At level three the infinitive can take il and behave as a masculine singular noun, mainly in written or set expressions such as con il passare del tempo, il continuo abbaiare del cane. Items test infinitive against gerund; which preposition (a, di, none) links the verb to the infinitive belongs to preposition-before-infinitive, so give the preposition in the sentence and do not blank it.

subs.label: sbagliando si impara, tornando a casa ho visto Luca: how, why, while
subs.focus: A gerund without stare says how (by doing), why (being, having) or during what other action the main action happens, and it is understood as done by the subject of the main verb. It takes no preposition: English by, while, on + -ing are already inside the gerund. Typical errors: a preposition before it (Ho imparato per guardando film; In tornando a casa), and the infinitive for by + -ing (Ho imparato l'italiano a guardare film). Items contrast gerund with infinitive and with preposition + gerund; keep to the simple gerund (no avendo fatto) and to sentences where both actions clearly have the same subject. Pronouns attached to the gerund belong to pronoun-position.

subs.label: mentre cucinavo è arrivato Luca: different subjects need a clause
subs.focus: When the -ing action has a different subject from the main verb, everyday Italian needs a clause with its own verb: mentre + imperfetto (or presente), or quando. A gerund would be read as the action of the main subject: Tornando a casa, ho visto Luca means I was the one going home. Typical error: Cucinando, è arrivato Luca for While I was cooking, Luca arrived, and Ho visto Luca tornando a casa meant as Luca was going home. Mentre + verb is also correct with the same subject (Mentre tornavo a casa, ho visto Luca), so items must make the subjects clearly different when the gerund is the wrong answer, and must never mark mentre + verb wrong just because the subjects match. Formal writing has gerunds with their own stated subject (Essendo il negozio chiuso, ...); do not test them.

subs.label: l'ho visto uscire, sento cantare i bambini: see / hear someone doing
subs.focus: After verbs of perception such as vedere, sentire, guardare, ascoltare, the action of the person or thing perceived is in the infinitive: Ho visto Maria uscire; Sento i bambini giocare. A gerund here would describe the one who sees or hears (Ho visto Maria uscendo: I saw Maria as I was going out). Typical error: the gerund copied from English saw her leaving, heard them singing. A relative clause is also correct (Ho visto Maria che usciva), so items offer infinitive against gerund and never mark che + verb wrong. Keep the perceived person as a noun or a simple lo / la / li / le before the verb of perception.

subs.label: la ragazza che parla, un film interessante: -ing describing a noun
subs.focus: English -ing that describes a noun is not a gerund in Italian. If it tells what the person or thing is doing, use a relative clause: la ragazza che parla con Luca, l'uomo che legge il giornale. If it is a quality, use the adjective in -ante or -ente where one exists, such as interessante, divertente, sorridente, seguente, bollente; these agree in number (film interessanti). Typical error: the gerund after a noun (la ragazza parlando con Luca, un film interessando). Not every verb has a usable -ante / -ente adjective (the girl speaking is not la ragazza parlante), so items give adjectives only from the common ones and otherwise expect che + verb.

rules.rule: For what is happening right now, use the presente of stare + gerund; for what was going on at a past moment, the imperfetto of stare + gerund. The verb is stare, not essere, and the gerund does not change.
rules.pattern: sto / stai / sta / stiamo / state / stanno + -ando / -endo; stavo / stavi / stava ... + -ando / -endo

examples.en: I am eating now.
What are you doing?
The children are sleeping.
When you called, I was driving.

rules.note: The simple tenses are also correct for an ongoing action (Che fai? Guardo la televisione); stare + gerundio just insists on in progress at this moment.

rules.rule: Do not put stare + gerundio in a compound tense. English have been / had been + -ing is a plain Italian tense.

examples.en: I have been working all day.
We have been walking for three hours.

examples.tl: Ieri ho studiato fino a mezzanotte.
examples.en: Yesterday I was studying until midnight.

rules.note: An action that started in the past and still continues takes the presente with da (Studio italiano da due anni); that use is drilled in time-expressions.

rules.rule: Take off -are and add -ando; take off -ere or -ire and add -endo. Verbs like finire and capire have no -isc- in the gerund.
rules.pattern: parlare: parlando; leggere: leggendo; partire: partendo; finire: finendo

examples.en: I am waiting for the bus.
Maria is reading a book.
We are finishing dinner.
The train is leaving.

rules.rule: A few short infinitives build the gerund on a longer stem, the same one as their imperfetto: fare, facendo; dire, dicendo; bere, bevendo; tradurre, traducendo.
rules.pattern: facevo: facendo; dicevo: dicendo; bevevo: bevendo

examples.en: What are you saying?
I am doing the shopping.

examples.tl: Stanno bevendo un caffè al bar.
examples.en: They are having a coffee at the café.

rules.note: Essere and avere are regular in form (essendo, avendo), and are mostly met as bare gerunds of cause (Essendo stanco, ...; Avendo fame, ...); essere is not used after stare.

rules.rule: For a plan or arrangement in the future, use the presente (or the futuro) with the time word. Stare + gerundio cannot point to tomorrow or next week.

examples.en: I am leaving for Milan tomorrow.
We are having dinner at Paola's tonight.

examples.tl: Sabato vado al mare con Luca.
examples.en: I am going to the seaside with Luca on Saturday.

rules.rule: States take a simple tense. Verbs such as sapere, conoscere, volere, potere, dovere, essere and avere for possession are not normally used with stare + gerundio, and English is wearing, is sitting are states too.

examples.en: Now I know the truth.

examples.tl: Oggi Anna porta un vestito rosso.
examples.en: Anna is wearing a red dress today.

examples.tl: Il nonno è seduto in giardino.
examples.en: Grandpa is sitting in the garden.
As a child I had a dog.

rules.note: Si sta sedendo is correct only for the movement of sitting down. Many verbs of thinking and feeling do accept stare + gerundio when they describe a passing activity (Sto pensando a te; Mi sto divertendo).

rules.rule: For about to, use stare per + infinitive: the action has not started yet. In the imperfetto it means was about to, usually before an interruption.
rules.pattern: sto per + infinitive; stavo per + infinitive

examples.en: The train is about to leave.

examples.tl: Sbrigati, il film sta per cominciare.
examples.en: Hurry up, the film is about to start.

examples.tl: Stavo per uscire quando ha telefonato Anna.
examples.en: I was about to go out when Anna phoned.
It is about to rain.

rules.note: Compare Il film sta cominciando: it is starting at this very moment.

rules.rule: When -ing names an activity, use the infinitive: as the subject of the sentence, after verbs such as piacere, amare, preferire, smettere di, finire di, and after prepositions such as senza and invece di.
rules.pattern: infinitive + verb; mi piace + infinitive; smettere di + infinitive; senza + infinitive

examples.en: Swimming is good for you.
I like reading in the evening.
I have stopped smoking.
He left without saying anything.

rules.note: With il the infinitive works as a masculine noun, mainly in writing and in set phrases: con il passare del tempo (with the passing of time), il continuo abbaiare del cane (the dog's constant barking). The plain infinitive without il is the everyday choice.

rules.rule: To say by doing, while doing or because of being, use the gerund alone, with no preposition. The person doing it is the subject of the main verb.

examples.en: You learn by making mistakes.
I learned Italian by watching films.

examples.tl: Tornando a casa ho visto Luca.
examples.en: On my way home I saw Luca.

examples.tl: Essendo stanco, sono andato a letto presto.
examples.en: Being tired, I went to bed early.

rules.rule: If the two actions have different subjects, do not use the gerund: use mentre (or quando) + a verb with its own subject. With the same subject, mentre + verb and the gerund are both correct.

examples.en: While I was cooking, Luca arrived.

examples.tl: Mentre i bambini dormono, io lavoro.
examples.en: While the children are sleeping, I work.

examples.tl: Mentre aspettavamo, ha cominciato a piovere.
examples.en: While we were waiting, it started to rain.

rules.note: Formal written Italian allows a gerund with its own stated subject (Essendo il negozio chiuso, siamo tornati a casa); in speech use a clause with perché, mentre or quando.

rules.rule: After verbs of seeing and hearing such as vedere, sentire, guardare, ascoltare, put what the other person does in the infinitive. A relative clause with che is also possible; the gerund is not, because it would describe the one who sees.
rules.pattern: vedere / sentire + person + infinitive; lo / la / li / le + vedere / sentire + infinitive

examples.en: I saw Maria leaving.

examples.tl: Sento i bambini giocare in giardino.
examples.en: I can hear the children playing in the garden.
I saw him going into the café.
I watch the people going by.

rules.note: Also correct: Ho visto Maria che usciva. Ho visto Maria uscendo is good Italian only with the meaning I saw Maria as I was going out.

rules.rule: When -ing describes a noun, use che + verb for what the person or thing is doing, or an adjective in -ante / -ente for a quality when a common one exists. Never put a gerund after the noun.
rules.pattern: noun + che + verb; noun + adjective in -ante / -ente

examples.tl: La ragazza che parla con Luca è mia sorella.
examples.en: The girl talking to Luca is my sister.

examples.tl: Conosci l'uomo che legge il giornale?
examples.en: Do you know the man reading the newspaper?

examples.tl: Ho visto un film molto interessante.
examples.en: I saw a very interesting film.
Careful, the water is boiling hot.

rules.note: Adjectives in -ante / -ente agree in number: un libro divertente, due libri divertenti. If you are not sure the adjective exists, the relative clause is always safe.

contrasts.why: The progressive is built with stare, not essere: sto, stai, sta + gerund.

right.en: I am leaving for Rome tomorrow.

contrasts.why: Stare + gerundio is for an action in progress now. A future plan with domani takes the presente or the futuro.
Sapere is a state, not an action in progress; states take the simple tense.
Fare builds its gerund on the long stem fac-, as in facevo: facendo.

right.en: The train is about to leave.

contrasts.why: After stare per comes the infinitive. Sta partendo, without per, would mean it is leaving right now.
An activity used as the subject of the sentence is an infinitive in Italian, never a gerund.
After piacere the activity is in the infinitive.

contrasts.wrong: Ho imparato l'italiano per guardando film.

right.en: I learned Italian by watching films.

contrasts.why: The gerund already means by doing; it takes no preposition before it.

right.en: While I was cooking, Luca arrived.

contrasts.why: A gerund is read with the subject of the main verb, so this would make Luca the cook. Different subjects need mentre + verb.

contrasts.wrong: La ragazza parlando con Luca è mia sorella.

right.tl: La ragazza che parla con Luca è mia sorella.
right.en: The girl talking to Luca is my sister.

contrasts.why: A gerund cannot describe a noun. Use che + verb.

cheat: Happening right now or at that moment: sto / stavo + -ando / -endo. Stare, never essere; never in a compound tense.
Tomorrow, next week, or a state (so, voglio, ho, è seduto): simple tense, no stare + gerundio.
-ing as a thing you do (subject, after piacere, after di or senza): infinitive.
By / while doing, same subject: gerund alone, no preposition. Different subject: mentre + verb.
See or hear someone doing: vedere / sentire + infinitive.
-ing describing a noun: che + verb, or an adjective like interessante.
